In [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] [[mathematics]], a '''Baxter permutation''' is a [[permutation]] <math>\sigma \in S_n</math> which satisfies the following generalized [[Permutation pattern|pattern avoidance]] property:
* There are no indices <math>i<j<k</math> such that <math>\sigma(j+1)<\sigma(i)<\sigma(k)<\sigma(j)</math> or <math>\sigma(j)<\sigma(k)<\sigma(i)<\sigma(j+1)</math>.
Equivalently, using the notation for [[vincular pattern]]s, a Baxter permutation is one that avoids the two dashed patterns <math>2-41-3</math> and <math>3-14-2</math>.

For example, the permutation <math>\sigma=2413</math> in <math>S_4</math> (written in [[one-line notation]]) is ''not'' a Baxter permutation because, taking 
<math>i= 1</math>, <math>j=2</math> and <math>k = 4</math>, this permutation violates the first condition.

These permutations were introduced by [[Glen E. Baxter]] in the context of [[mathematical analysis]].<ref>{{citation |last1=Baxter |first1=Glen |title=On fixed points of the composite of commuting functions |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=851–855 |year=1964 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1964-015-06/S0002-9939-1964-0184217-8/S0002-9939-1964-0184217-8.pdf |doi=10.2307/2034894 |jstor=2034894 |doi-access=free}}.</ref>

== Enumeration ==
For <math>n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots</math>, the number <math>a_n</math> of Baxter permutations of length <math>n</math> is 
<blockquote>1, 2, 6, 22, 92, 422, 2074, 10754, 58202, 326240, 1882960, 11140560, 67329992, 414499438, 2593341586, 16458756586, ... {{oeis|A001181}} </blockquote>
In general, <math>a_n</math> has the following formula:<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chung | first1 = F. R. K. | author1-link = Fan Chung
 | last2 = Graham | first2 = R. L. | author2-link = Ronald Graham
 | last3 = Hoggatt | first3 = V. E. Jr.| author3-link = Verner Emil Hoggatt, Jr.
 | last4 = Kleiman | first4 = M.
 | doi = 10.1016/0097-3165(78)90068-7
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
 | mr = 491652
 | pages = 382–394
 | series = Series A
 | title = The number of Baxter permutations
 | url = http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/78_08_baxter.pdf
 | volume = 24
 | year = 1978| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>
<math display=block>
a_n \, = \,\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1}}{\binom{n+1}{1}\binom{n+1}{2}}
.</math>
In fact, this formula is graded by the number of [[Permutation#Ascents, descents, runs and excedances|descents]] in the permutations, i.e., there are <math>\frac{\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1}}{\binom{n+1}{1}\binom{n+1}{2}}</math> Baxter permutations in <math>S_n</math> with <math>k-1</math> descents.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dulucq | first1 = S.
 | last2 = Guibert | first2 = O.
 | doi = 10.1016/S0012-365X(97)00112-X
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1603713
 | pages = 143–156
 | title = Baxter permutations
 | volume = 180
 | year = 1998| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

== Other properties ==
* The number of [[Alternating permutation|alternating]] Baxter permutations of length <math>2n</math> is <math>(C_n)^2</math>, the square of a [[Catalan number]], and of length <math>2n+1</math> is 
<math>C_n C_{n+1}</math>.
* The number of doubly alternating Baxter permutations of length <math>2n</math> and <math>2n+1</math> (i.e., those for which both <math>\sigma</math> and its inverse <math>\sigma^{-1}</math> are alternating) is the Catalan number <math>C_n</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Guibert | first1 = Olivier
 | last2 = Linusson | first2 = Svante
 | doi = 10.1016/S0012-365X(99)00261-7
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1766265
 | pages = 157–166
 | title = Doubly alternating Baxter permutations are Catalan
 | volume = 217
 | year = 2000| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

==Motivation: commuting functions==
Baxter introduced Baxter permutations while studying the [[Common fixed point problem|fixed points of commuting continuous functions]].  In particular, if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are continuous functions from the interval <math>[0, 1]</math> to itself such that <math>f(g(x)) = g(f(x))</math> for all <math>x</math>, and <math>f(g(x)) = x</math> for finitely many 
<math>x</math> in <math>[0, 1]</math>, then:
* the number of these fixed points is odd; 
* if the fixed points are <math>x_1  < x_2< \ldots < x_{2k + 1}</math> then <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> act as mutually-inverse permutations on 
<math>\{x_1,x_3, \ldots, x_{2k + 1} \} </math> and <math>\{x_2, x_4,\ldots, x_{2k} \}</math>;
* the permutation induced by <math>f</math> on <math>\{x_1, x_3, \ldots, x_{2k+1}\}</math> uniquely determines the permutation induced by 
<math>f</math> on <math>\{ x_2, x_4, \ldots, x_{2k}\}</math>;
* under the natural relabeling <math>x_1\to 1</math>, <math>x_3\to 2</math>, etc., the permutation induced on <math>\{1, 2, \ldots, k + 1\}</math> is a Baxter permutation.
